d: Full mock interview: design a web crawler in 45 minutes
goal: Your win today: you can run the whole interview without notes, from scoping and 400/800 pages/s and 30 PB, through the pipeline and workflow, the two-layer URL frontier, downloader speed-ups and robustness, to traps, extensibility and a clean wrap-up.
bookSections: Whole chapter via the 4-step framework: Step 1 scope, traits, estimates; Step 2 components and workflow; Step 3 BFS vs DFS, URL frontier (politeness, priority, freshness, storage), HTML downloader (robots.txt, performance), robustness, extensibility, problematic content; Step 4 wrap up

stages.title: Scope it
stages.teaches: Requirements: search engine indexing; 1 billion pages/month; HTML only; pick up new and edited pages; store HTML up to 5 years; ignore duplicate content. Traits: scalability, robustness, politeness, extensibility. Estimates: ~400 pages/s, ~800 peak, 500 TB/month at 500 KB/page, 30 PB over 5 years.
stages.interaction: Interview chat UI like 0008: the interviewer bubble says 'Design a web crawler.' The learner has 6 'question tokens' and a deck of 11 questions (6 strong, 3 weak, 2 premature-implementation like 'Kafka or RabbitMQ?'). Strong picks get the interviewer's reply pinned to a requirement board; weak picks spend a token with a coach note. Then a 'traits' quick-pick (choose 4 of 7: scalable, robust, polite, extensible + distractors 'real-time', 'strongly consistent', 'serverless'). Then a rapid estimate round: 4 multiple-choice estimates (avg QPS, peak QPS, monthly storage, 5-year storage), each with 3 options within an order of magnitude and a 'show work' toggle.
stages.check: Board holds the 6 requirements, 4 traits picked, 4 estimates correct (retry allowed). Scorecard records wasted tokens.

stages.title: Sketch it
stages.sub: Step 2 · high-level design and buy-in (10–15 min)
stages.teaches: Seed URLs → URL Frontier → HTML Downloader (+ DNS Resolver) → Content Parser → Content Seen? (→ Content Storage) → URL Extractor → URL Filter → URL Seen? (→ URL Storage) → back to URL Frontier.
stages.interaction: Whiteboard builder: 14 tiles (the 11 real components plus distractors 'Load balancer for users', 'Redis pub/sub', 'GraphQL gateway') to drag onto a canvas and connect with arrows. Minimum correct: all 11 components wired in the right order, with storage boxes hanging off the two seen-checks and the loop closing back to the frontier. Distractors get a 'what's that for here?' note and don't block progress. Then the interviewer asks two buy-in questions inline: 'Why compare hashes in Content Seen?' and 'What would you use for URL Seen?' (choose from chips: Bloom filter / hash table / SQL LIKE query / linear scan; first two accepted, and choosing Bloom filter triggers 'and its downside?' → false positives skip some new URLs).
stages.check: Diagram has the 11 components wired correctly and both buy-in questions answered.

stages.title: Dig in
stages.teaches: BFS over DFS, but BFS alone is impolite and priority-blind; front queues (prioritizer, f1…fn, biased selector) + back queues (router, host→queue mapping, b1…bn, selector, one worker per queue, delay); freshness by update history and importance; frontier on disk with memory buffers; robots.txt checked first and cached; distributed crawl, DNS cache (10–200 ms lookups), locality, short timeouts; consistent hashing, saved state, exception handling, data validation.
stages.interaction: Three deep-dive panels the interviewer 'zooms into'. (a) Frontier: an empty two-layer frame; the learner drags 8 frontier parts into the front or back half, then answers 'Which half stops us hammering wikipedia.com?' (back). (b) Downloader: a 'slow crawl' profile chart (bars for DNS wait, far-away hosts, dead hosts, robots.txt refetches); the learner assigns a fix to each bar from chips (DNS cache, locality, short timeout, cache robots.txt). (c) Pushback round: the interviewer challenges two choices the learner made earlier, e.g. 'Your Bloom filter says a brand-new URL was seen; now what?' (accept small loss / size it for target false-positive rate) and 'One downloader host dies: whose URLs move?' (only its arc on the consistent-hash ring).
stages.check: All three panels answered; at least one accepted mitigation per pushback.

stages.title: Boss: the curveball barrage
stages.teaches: Failure and extension follow-ups across the whole design.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'frontier', label:'Frontier fix', sub:'priority · politeness · freshness'}, {k:'download', label:'Downloader fix', sub:'robots · DNS · locality · timeout'}, {k:'robust', label:'Robustness fix', sub:'hashing · checkpoints · exceptions'}, {k:'content', label:'Content fix', sub:'dedupe · traps · noise · render'}]. Scenarios (10): 'A site owner emails that our bot is overloading their server' → frontier (back queues / delay); 'The crawler wastes its first month on spam forums' → frontier (prioritizer) and mention anti-spam; 'Half our fetch time is name lookups' → download (DNS cache); 'A crawl server crashes; on reboot the crawl starts from scratch' → robust (save state); 'Indexed product pages on JavaScript-heavy shops have no links' → content (render first); 'One host has produced 50M URLs in a day' → content (spider trap guard); 'We add 10 downloader servers and every host gets reassigned' → robust (consistent hashing); 'Stale news results: homepages revisited monthly' → frontier (freshness); 'Threads stuck for minutes on servers that never answer' → download (short timeout); 'The same syndicated story is being stored from 300 different news sites' → content (hash-based dedupe in Content Seen?).

stages.title: Wrap it up
stages.teaches: Wrap-up: recap the four traits (scalable, polite, extensible, robust); then extras: server-side (dynamic) rendering, anti-spam filtering of unwanted pages, database replication and sharding, horizontal scaling with stateless servers, availability/consistency/reliability, analytics. Plus honest call-outs: exact hashes miss near-duplicates; Bloom false positives skip some URLs; politeness should also be per IP.
stages.interaction: Pick-5 from 10 wrap-up cards against a soft 30-second timer (running out only adds a scorecard note). Strong: render JavaScript before parsing; anti-spam filter; DB replication + sharding; stateless crawl servers for horizontal scaling; analytics; near-duplicate detection caveat; per-IP politeness caveat. Weak: 'rewrite in Rust', 'add a mobile app', 'switch to GraphQL'. The interviewer reacts to each pick.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: The whole chapter as one answer.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'You have 90 seconds. Summarise your web crawler design.' Model: 'Scope: a crawler for search indexing, a billion HTML pages a month, picking up new and changed pages, keeping the HTML five years and skipping duplicates. That's about 400 pages a second, 800 at peak, 500 TB a month and 30 PB over five years. It must be scalable, robust, polite and extensible. Pipeline: seed URLs feed the URL frontier; downloaders resolve DNS and fetch; a parser validates; Content Seen? hashes pages to drop duplicates; new pages are stored and their links extracted, made absolute, filtered, and checked against URL Seen?, a Bloom filter, before going back into the frontier. The frontier has front queues for priority, scored by things like PageRank and change rate with a biased random selector, and back queues for politeness: one host per queue, one worker per queue, a delay between requests. We recrawl by update history and importance, and keep the frontier on disk with memory buffers. Downloaders obey cached robots.txt, are distributed by consistent hashing on host, cache DNS, sit near the sites they crawl and use short timeouts. We checkpoint state, handle exceptions per page and validate data. We cap URL length and review abnormal sites for spider traps, filter noise and spam, plug in modules for new content types, and render JavaScript for dynamic sites.' Checks: ['Scope and the four estimates', 'Four traits', 'Full pipeline including both seen-checks', 'Front queues for priority and back queues for politeness', 'Downloader speed-ups and robustness measures', 'Traps, noise, extensibility and rendering']. After the drill, show a scorecard summarising tokens used, diagram accuracy, boss score and wrap-up picks, saved under a separate key 'sdq:v1:0906-interview' like 0008.

caveats: The book's design is a teaching model built on Mercator-era ideas (late 1990s). Modern crawlers add JavaScript rendering pipelines, near-duplicate fingerprints, per-IP and adaptive rate limits, and machine-learned priority, but the skeleton (frontier, fetch, parse, dedupe, extract, filter, seen-check) is the same.

The interview prompt usually doesn't need indexing, ranking or search serving. Say explicitly that those are downstream consumers of Content Storage and out of scope, so the interviewer knows you know where the crawler ends.
Interviewers often probe one area hard (most commonly the URL frontier's politeness and priority). It's fine to skim the rest and go deep where they push.
